docs.title: systemspec-runbook
docs.text:
A runbook as data: phases of steps, each with an owner, its dependencies, the actions that do it, the sentence that says when it is done, and typed checks that prove it.

A Go program declares the runbook from its own facts, so hosts, ports and counts are read, never typed twice. systemspec-runbook then:

  • validates it, reporting every problem together;
  • renders it as a Markdown page whose links are computed;
  • records what was done in an event log, and derives where each step stands: blocked, ready, in-progress, done or verified;
  • describes both as JSON Schemas generated from the Go types.

Start with Getting Started. The design documents explain the model and what comes next.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: go get github.com/plexusone/systemspec-runbook

docs.title: Declare a Runbook
docs.text:
A runbook has phases, and a phase has steps. Each step has:

Field Holds id <phase>.<n>, such as 1.2 owner operator, agent or both: the agent prepares, the operator runs, the agent checks dependsOn Steps that must be done first; nothing is implied by order actions What to do: Markdown text, an optional command, an optional owner and link done The sentence that says when the step is done checks Typed checks that prove it credentials IDs of the credentials the step creates gate Whether the step is a decision or condition rather than work

The package example, runbookspec/example_test.go, declares a two-step runbook, validates it, records an event, derives each step's state and renders the page.

docs.title: Link Without Typing Anchors
docs.text:
In any Markdown text:

  • [[step:1.2]] links to step 1.2, and [[step:1.2|the cut-over]] with your own text.
  • [[key|text]] links to a target your resolver returns, such as a section of another generated page:
page, err := rb.Markdown(runbookspec.RenderOptions{
    Resolve: func(key string) (string, error) {
        return sections[key], nil // e.g. "plan.md#3-payments"
    },
    VerifyCommand: "bin/ops verify {step}",
    Generator:     "make runbook",
})

BrokenLinks(path, page) then reports any relative link whose file or heading does not exist, so a test can keep the page honest.

docs.title: Record Progress
docs.text:
log, err := runbookspec.LoadLog("events.json", rb.ID) // missing is empty
err = log.Append(rb, runbookspec.Event{Step: "1.1", Type: runbookspec.EventDone, At: time.Now(), By: runbookspec.OwnerOperator})
data, err := log.Marshal() // commit it with the work
Event Leaves the step started, failed in-progress done, skipped done verified verified: its checks passed reopened as if it had no events

A step with no events is blocked until its dependencies are done or verified, then ready. A note that looks like a secret is refused.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Declare each value known only at run time, and reference it as {{name}} in text, commands and checks:

rb.Variables = []runbookspec.Variable{
    {Name: "profile", Description: "the AWS profile", Env: "AWS_PROFILE"},
    {Name: "staticIp", Description: "the instance's address"},
}

Values come from --var name=value, then from sources the host registers, then from the declared environment variable, then from the variable's own command. The page shows each as <name>.

A variable can name the command that gives it, so a runbook kept as JSON reads a value with no Go code:

{Name: "staticIp", Description: "the instance's address", Later: true,
    From: &runbookspec.Exec{
        Args: []string{"pulumi", "stack", "output", "staticIp", "--stack", "prod"},
        Dir:  "stack",
        Env:  map[string]string{"AWS_PROFILE": "{{profile}}"},
    }},

The command runs only when the value is first needed, without a shell, in --root or its dir; its trimmed output is the value. If it fails or prints nothing, the variable stays unfilled, the error says why, and the command runs again the next time. Later lets a run start before the stack exists.

docs.title: Commands a Run Executes
docs.text:
Command is shown for a person to adapt; Exec is what run executes: a program and its arguments, never through a shell.

Action{
    Owner: runbookspec.OwnerOperator,
    Text:  "Create the stack and set the master password.",
    Exec: []runbookspec.Exec{
        {Args: []string{"pulumi", "stack", "init", "prod"}, Dir: "stack",
            Env: map[string]string{"AWS_PROFILE": "{{profile}}"}},
        {Args: []string{"pulumi", "config", "set", "--secret", "db:password"}, Dir: "stack",
            Env:   map[string]string{"AWS_PROFILE": "{{profile}}"},
            Stdin: &runbookspec.Stdin{RandomHex: 32}},
    },
}

Stdin.RandomHex generates the password in Go and pipes it in, so it is never shown and never in a process's arguments; Stdin.From pipes another command's output in, as a | b would. The page shows the shell lines a person would type: cd stack, export AWS_PROFILE=<profile>, openssl rand -hex 32 | pulumi config set --secret db:password.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
checker := &runbookspec.Checker{
    Values: values,
    Named: map[string]runbookspec.NamedFunc{
        "aws.bucket": func(ctx context.Context, args map[string]string) (string, error) {
            // return nil when so, an error wrapping ErrSkip when you cannot tell
        },
    },
}
results := checker.Step(ctx, rb.Step("1.1"))

dns, http, unreachable and command checks need no registration. VerifyEvent turns results into verified, or failed for a done step that no longer passes.

docs.title: Run a Step
docs.text:
runbookspec run 1.2 --runbook runbook.json --var profile=ops

The run refuses a blocked step, fills every variable before anything runs, asks before each command (--yes to skip asking), waits for a person's steps, stops at the first failure, records started, failed and done, and then runs the checks and records verified. Another owner's action is confirmed as done, never run.

docs.title: Schemas
docs.text: schema.Runbook() and schema.Events() return the embedded JSON Schemas. After changing the types, regenerate them with go generate ./schema.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
Each release has its own notes. The full changelog, generated from CHANGELOG.json, is CHANGELOG.md in the repository.

Version Date Highlights v0.2.0 2026-11-22 HTML pages built with templ: full width, steps as sections with owner badges, copy buttons on commands v0.1.0 2026-11-22 The first release: the runbook model, state from an event log, typed checks, variables, guided runs, and Markdown and HTML pages

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text: The first release. A runbook is data: phases of steps, each with an owner, its dependencies, the actions that do it, the sentence that says when it is done, and typed checks that prove it. A program declares it from its own facts; systemspec-runbook validates it, renders it, records what was done, derives where each step stands, and runs it step by step.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• The model. Phases and steps with an owner (operator, agent or both), dependencies, actions, a done sentence, checks, and the credentials a step creates. Validation reports every problem at once.
  • State from an event log. Each step is blocked, ready, in-progress, done or verified, derived from its dependencies and the log.
  • Typed checks. dns, http, unreachable, command, and named checks a host registers in Go. Checks only read, and report pass, fail with what they saw, or skip with why.
  • Variables. {{name}} in text, commands and checks, filled from flags, a host's providers, the environment, or a command the variable declares.
  • Guided runs. run <step> shows each action with its variables filled, asks before each command and runs it without a shell, waits for a person's steps, stops at the first failure, records the step and runs its checks. A new secret is generated in Go and piped straight to the program that stores it.
  • Pages. Markdown, with links to steps and resolved targets so no anchor is typed by hand, and a check for broken relative links. HTML, as a page styled for light and dark themes or as its body for a host's page; raw HTML in a runbook's text is never passed through, and placeholders such as <value> are shown.
  • Commands. The Cobra commands a host tool mounts (validate, list, show, record, verify, run, doc, schema), with an events flag a host can rename, and runbookspec, the same commands over a runbook kept as JSON.
  • Schemas. JSON Schemas of a runbook and its event log, generated from the Go types and embedded.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: A module that required a pseudo-version of systemspec-runbook can require v0.1.0 instead; nothing else changes.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text: HTML pages are built from the runbook with templ components rather than converted from the Markdown page, so the HTML has a layout of its own while the Markdown page stays as it is.

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • Copy buttons. Every code block on the HTML page has a button that copies its command for pasting into a terminal, with the clipboard API, or a selection where a page opened from a file cannot use it. Script is the script, for a host that places the fragment in its own page.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The HTML page uses the window's full width. The phase summary is a table; each step is a section with its owner's badge (operator, agent or both), its dependencies linked, its actions numbered with their own owners' badges and their commands escaped in code blocks, then the credentials it creates, when it is done and its checks.
  • Anchors are the Markdown page's, so [[step:1.2]] links and the links in a runbook's text land on the same step on both pages.
  • Text fields are still Markdown, converted with goldmark without passing raw HTML through, and placeholders such as <value> are shown.
  • Style is the full-width sheet with the step and badge styles, for a host that places the fragment in its own page.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: • Requires github.com/a-h/templ v0.3.1118. go generate ./runbookspec regenerates the components with that version.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: No code change is needed: HTML, HTMLOptions and Style keep their names. A host that places the fragment adds Script after it for the copy buttons. A host that styled the old page's elements should check its rules against the new structure.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
1. The model. Types, validation, the event log, derived state, rendering, link checks and schemas: enough for a program to declare a runbook, generate its page and record progress.
  2. Checks. The runner and the generic checks, then recording verify results, so every step can be checked.
  3. Command line. Commands over JSON files, and Cobra commands a host tool mounts over its own runbook.
  4. Release. A documentation site and the first release, once the model has run a real launch from start to end.

docs.title: Working Rules
docs.text:
• Declared by the program that uses it. A runbook is built in Go from the user's own facts, so hosts, ports and counts are never typed twice.
  • A check for every step, including the ones a person does.
  • Public-ready from the first commit: examples and tests use neutral names.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: A runbook as data: phases of steps, each with an owner, its dependencies, the actions that do it, the sentence that says when it is done, and typed checks that prove it. A Go program declares the runbook; systemspec-runbook validates it, renders it as a Markdown page, records what was done in an event log, derives where each step stands, and runs its checks.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
• Runbooks are prose. "Done when the zone is active" is read, not run. Whether a step still holds after an incident is checked by hand, by whoever remembers how.
  • Pages drift from the tools. A runbook names commands, hosts, ports and sections of other generated pages; nothing checks they still match.
  • Progress is not recorded. Which steps are done, by whom and when, lives in a chat or a person's memory.
  • Steps repeat. A second environment, a second site or a rebuild runs most of the same steps, typed again from the page.

docs.title: Users
docs.text: User Needs An operator What to do next, the exact commands, a check of the result, and a record of what was done A coding agent working beside the operator The same steps, owners and checks, to prepare work, verify it and record it without handling secrets A reader after an incident A check of everything the runbook set up, and the history of when it was done

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. A typed model of runbooks, phases, steps, actions, links and checks, with validation that reports every problem together.
  2. A generated page in Markdown, whose links to steps and to other generated pages are computed, never typed.
  3. An event log of what happened to each step, with each step's state derived from its events and its dependencies.
  4. Checks that can be run for every step, including steps a person does in a console: DNS answers, HTTP statuses, addresses that must not answer, command results, and checks a program registers by name.
  5. JSON Schemas of a runbook and of its log, generated from the types.
  6. Guided runs. A step's commands run from the runbook itself, with its variables filled and each command confirmed, console steps waited on, progress recorded and the checks run after, so nothing is copied by hand.
  7. A command line over JSON files, and Cobra commands a host tool mounts over its own runbook.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• A workflow engine. Nothing runs steps on a schedule or on its own; a person or an agent starts each one, and a guided run confirms each command unless told the step is rehearsed.
  • A shell. Commands are programs and arguments; pipes and generated values are structured, so a run behaves the same on every platform.
  • Secrets. No type holds a value; checks read names, settings and public answers; the log refuses notes that look like secrets.
  • Automating console steps. A step done once in a console keeps an instruction and gains a check.

docs.title: Success Measures
docs.text:
• A real launch is run from a runbook declared with it, and its checks say where the launch stands at any time.
  • A second environment is set up from the same runbook with no step typed from prose that has a command.
  • The rendered page has no broken links, by test.

docs.title: systemspec-runbook: Roadmap
docs.text: Items carry stable IDs; phase status is derived from its items.

  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-003 Markdown rendering with computed links, and link checks
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-004 JSON Schemas of a runbook and its log, generated from the types

docs.text:
• [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-005 The check runner: named checks registered in Go, ${name} variables, and pass, fail and skip results
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-006 Generic checks: dns, http, unreachable and command
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-007 Recording verify results: verified for steps that pass, failed for done steps that no longer do

docs.text:
• [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-012 Variables: declared {{name}} references in text, commands and checks, filled from flags, the environment or providers the host registers, such as a stack's outputs; a step cannot run with one unfilled
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-013 Executable actions: a program and its arguments with a directory and environment, never through a shell; standard input from another command or from a random value generated in Go and never shown
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-014 Guided run of a step: refuse a blocked step, show each action with its variables filled, confirm and run commands, wait on console steps, stop at the first failure, record started, failed and done, then run the checks and record verified
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-008 Cobra commands a host tool mounts: list, show, record, verify, run, doc, schema

  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-018 HTML from templ components: the runbook rendered straight to a full-width page, steps as sections with owner badges, anchors shared with the Markdown page
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-017 A host's events flag: the commands' event log flag renamed when the host has an events flag of its own
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMSPECRUNBOOK-015 Variables from commands: a variable names the command whose output is its value, such as a stack's output, so a runbook kept as JSON runs with runbookspec and no host code; --root sets where commands run

docs.title: systemspec-runbook: Technical Requirements
docs.text: Design for PRD.md. Process is in PLAN.md; work items are in ROADMAP.md.

docs.title: 1. Packages
docs.text:
Package Holds runbookspec The model, validation, the event log and derived state, rendering and link checks; the check runner and generic checks schema The JSON Schemas of a runbook and its log, generated from the types and embedded cli Cobra commands a host tool mounts over its own runbook: validate, list, show, record, verify, run, doc, schema cmd/runbookspec The same commands over a runbook kept as JSON

runbookspec depends only on the standard library; schema adds invopop/jsonschema and oscompat; cli adds Cobra.

docs.title: 2. The Model
docs.text:
• Runbook: an ID, a title, a summary, how to use it, phases, and the work that follows it.
  • Phase: a number, a title, what finishing it gives, and its steps.
  • Step: an ID <phase>.<n>, a title, an owner (operator, agent or both), the steps it depends on, actions, the sentence that says when it is done, the IDs of the credentials it creates, whether it is a gate, and its checks.
  • Action: Markdown text, an optional shell command shown as a code block, an optional owner, and an optional link resolved at render time.
  • Check: an ID, a description, and a kind with exactly the matching parameters: dns (name, type, substrings the answers contain), http (URL, status, body or redirect location), unreachable (address and timeout), command (arguments, run without a shell), or named (a check registered in Go, with string arguments). Parameters may hold {{name}} variables, filled at run time.
  • Exec: what a guided run executes: a program and its arguments, a directory relative to the runbook's root, and environment variables; standard input from another command or from a random value. Never a shell, so a run behaves the same on every platform. The page shows the shell lines a person would type to do the same.
  • Variable: a name, a description, an optional environment variable, an example, and an optional command whose output is its value. Every {{name}} in the runbook must be declared, and a variable never holds a secret.

Validation checks unique IDs, owners, that dependencies exist and come earlier, that each check has exactly its kind's parameters, and, through options, that credential IDs and named checks are known.

docs.title: 3. Events and State
docs.text: An event is a step, a type (started, done, verified, failed, skipped, reopened), a time, who, and a note that must not look like a secret. A step's state is derived by replaying its events: started and failed leave it in-progress, done and skipped leave it done, verified leaves it verified, and reopened clears it. A step with no state is blocked while a dependency is not done or verified, and ready otherwise.

docs.title: 4. Rendering
docs.text: Markdown writes the page: the summary, how to use it, a table of phases, each step with its owner, dependencies, actions, credentials, when it is done and its checks, and the work that follows. In text, [[step:<id>]] links to a step and [[<key>|text]] to a target the caller's resolver returns. Slug names headings as MkDocs does, and BrokenLinks reports relative links whose file or heading does not exist.

docs.title: 5. Variables
docs.text: Values fill variables from sources in order: --var name=value flags, then providers the host registers, then each variable's declared environment variable, then the variable's own command (from), such as pulumi stack output staticIp. That command runs without a shell, in the runbook's root or its dir, only when the value is first needed; its trimmed standard output is the value. When it fails or prints nothing the variable stays unfilled, the error names why, and the command runs again the next time, so a value an earlier command of the run creates is found. Validation refuses a command that reads standard input, references an undeclared variable, or needs its own value through other variables' commands. A command with an unfilled variable never runs: the run names every missing value first. The page shows a variable as <name>.

docs.title: 6. Checks
docs.text: A Checker runs checks with a registry of named checks and the values. Each returns pass, fail with what it saw, or skip with why: a check whose variable is unfilled, whose program is missing, or whose named check wraps ErrSkip, skips and says so; a skip is never a pass. Checks only read. VerifyEvent decides what a verify records: verified when every check passed, failed when a check fails on a step that was done, and nothing otherwise.

docs.title: 7. Guided Runs
docs.text:
Runner.Run runs one step:

  1. It refuses a blocked step unless forced (the started event says so), and asks before running a step that is already done again.
  2. It fills every command's variables before anything runs or is recorded.
  3. It records started, then shows each action. A command of the runner's owner, or of both, is shown as its shell line and run after a yes (or at once with --yes); another owner's action, or one with no command, waits for a yes that it is done.
  4. A declined command or action stops the run; the step stays in progress. A failing command records failed with the command and stops.
  5. After the last action it records done, runs the checks, and records what VerifyEvent decides.

Commands' standard input is the terminal, so a program's own questions work; the runner reads its own answers one byte at a time so it never takes input meant for a command. A random value is generated with crypto/rand and piped in, never shown or passed as an argument.

docs.title: 8. Security
docs.text:
• No type holds a secret's value, and no check reads one.
  • The log refuses notes matching key material, tokens and long random strings.
  • Commands, in checks and in runs, run without a shell; a generated secret is piped into the program that stores it, never put in its arguments.
